text: El Peñol is a town and municipality in the Antioquia Department of Colombia, with a population of 16,223 as recorded in the 2018 census. It is situated in the Eastern Antioquia subregion and is nationally recognized for the nearby monolith, also known as El Peñol, which serves as a major tourist attraction. The town was originally established in 1714 along the Negro-Nare River by Fray Miguel de Castro y Rivadeneiro, while the area had previously been inhabited by the indigenous Tahamí people before Spanish colonization. In 1971, Empresas Públicas de Medellín decided to dam the Negro-Nare River at Guatape to supply additional water and power to the rapidly expanding city of Medellín, located about 50 miles (30 km) to the west, leading to the flooding of the river valley where El Peñol was situated. The original town was taken by eminent domain, and a new town was constructed several miles west, displacing several thousand residents who were forced to relocate without legal recourse. The dam was completed and the valley flooded in 1978, resulting in the creation of the El Peñol-Guatapé Reservoir, which now covers the former site of El Peñol. A cross marks the location above the former parish of El Viejo Peñol that once fronted the town plaza, and some rural areas of Guatape were also submerged and lost. El Peñol has a subtropical highland climate (Köppen classification: Cfb), characterized by consistently warm temperatures and abundant rainfall.
